content: The study investigated the risk factors and predictors of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) relapse in patients co-infected with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in Ethiopia. The median age of the study population was 32 years, with a range of 28 to 39 years. The treatment regimen included a combination of liposomal amphotericin B (Amphotericin B, Gilead Sciences) at a total dose of 30 mg/kg, divided into six infusions of 5 mg/kg administered on alternate days, and oral miltefosine (Impavido, Paladin Labs, Montreal, Canada) for 28 days at a dose of 100 mg/day. Tuberculosis co-infection at the time of VL diagnosis was identified as a predictor of initial parasitological failure. However, there was no statistically significant association between high tissue parasite load (parasite grade 6+) at VL diagnosis and initial parasitological failure. Additionally, a history of prior VL treatment was not significantly associated with initial parasitological failure. The rates of initial parasitological failure were very low with the combination therapy of amphotericin B and miltefosine, suggesting that this regimen is an effective treatment option. Knowledge of predictors of poor outcomes, such as high tissue parasite load or tuberculosis co-infection, can aid in better management of these patients. Being on antiretroviral therapy (ART) at the time of VL diagnosis or initiating ART promptly was associated with a lower risk of VL relapse. Patients with high tissue parasite loads or those not on ART were at an increased risk of relapse. These high-risk patients should be prioritized for secondary prophylaxis and regular medical follow-up. Timely initiation of ART in all co-infected patients is critical to improving outcomes. The study highlights the importance of targeted interventions and close monitoring to reduce the risk of VL relapse in HIV co-infected individuals.
